note: Brain-chemistry systems shown in the Emotion view. Every statement cites records in data/evidence/sources.json. The emotion estimate (valence/arousal) is checked against listener ratings (data/emotion/valence_arousal.json); how strongly each system is engaged is NOT measured anywhere - it applies the cited findings to the estimated emotion and to musical events, and is labelled as such.

systems.name: Reward & pleasure
systems.chemicals: Dopamine, plus the brain's own opioids
systems.summary: In people who like the music, pleasurable moments - above all build-ups and the peaks they lead to - go with dopamine release in the striatum.
drivers: Build-ups (crescendos) and the peaks they lead to: sudden loudness changes and new instruments entering
A steady beat at a danceable tempo (groove)
Only in listeners who enjoy the music: it is scaled by your answer to "Do you like it?"

regions.role: Peak pleasure: dopamine release was measured here at the most intense moments.
Anticipation: dopamine release here in the build-up before a peak.
Groove: the pleasurable urge to move engages motor and reward parts of the striatum.
Valuing pleasure: activity changed with how intense music chills were.
Home of the midbrain dopamine neurons; midbrain activity rose with chills. The atlas has no separate midbrain, so the whole brainstem is lit.

evidence.says: PET showed dopamine release in the striatum during intensely pleasurable music: the caudate during anticipation, the nucleus accumbens at the peak.
Raising dopamine with a drug increased musical pleasure and blocking it reduced pleasure (27 people): dopamine causally contributes.
Blocking opioid receptors dulled emotional responses to music, so opioids are part of the pleasure system too.
Chills most often follow crescendos, sudden dynamic changes, roughness and new instruments or voices entering.
Loudness rose around chills, but the same passage did not give everyone chills (38 listeners).
Groove (wanting to move to the beat) engaged motor and reward networks.
Across 47 studies, pleasant music engaged the ventral and dorsal striatum, orbitofrontal cortex, insula and other reward areas.
Some healthy people get little pleasure from music at all (musical anhedonia) while money still rewards them.

caveats: Dopamine was measured in people hearing music they chose and loved. Nobody can measure your dopamine from a file; this shows moments of the kind that went with release in those listeners.
Chills and pleasure depend heavily on the listener, familiarity and mood.

systems.name: Stress & tension
systems.chemicals: Stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) and a faster heartbeat
systems.summary: Tense, harsh or unpleasant music and sudden loud hits engage threat-related areas such as the amygdala, and fast music speeds up breathing and heart rate. Evidence that music raises stress hormones is weak.
drivers: Tense, dark-and-energetic moments (negative valence with high arousal)
Fast tempo raises heart rate and breathing

regions.role: Responds to unpleasant, dissonant music - and also to joyful music, so it is not simply a fear centre.
Contains the hypothalamus, which starts the stress-hormone response. Not measured in music studies: shown as an extrapolation.

evidence.says: Unpleasant, dissonant music engaged the amygdala, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus and temporal poles.
The superficial amygdala responded to both fear-evoking and joyful music (in opposite directions).
Faster music raised breathing, heart rate and blood pressure; pauses brought them below baseline (24 people).
Across 104 trials, music interventions lowered heart rate and stress hormones on average - the calming direction.
Music has been linked to cortisol and other stress hormones, but mostly in small studies.

caveats: Tense music on screen or in a song is often enjoyed; perceiving tension is not the same as being stressed.
No study measured stress hormones moment by moment during a song.

systems.name: Sadness & reflection
systems.summary: Sad, slow, soft music engages memory and emotion areas such as the hippocampus and amygdala.
drivers: Sad moments: negative valence with low arousal (slow, soft, minor, dark)

regions.role: Engaged by sad music (and by music-evoked emotion generally).
Engaged by sad music together with the hippocampus.

evidence.says: Sad classical music engaged the hippocampus/amygdala region; happy music engaged the striatum (16 people scanned).

caveats: Many people enjoy sad music; sadness in the music does not mean the listener feels sad.

systems.name: Calm & relaxation
systems.chemicals: Body level: slower heartbeat and breathing; lower stress hormones in some studies
systems.summary: Slow, soft, pleasant music tends to slow breathing and heart rate. It is not tied to one brain area, so nothing on the brain lights for it.
drivers: Calm moments: positive valence with low arousal (slow, soft, consonant)

evidence.says: Music interventions lowered heart rate (d = 0.46) and stress hormones (d = 0.35) on average across 104 trials.
Slow music and pauses lowered breathing and heart rate.
But after a lab stressor, listening to music did not significantly speed recovery (14 studies).
Relaxing music before a stressor sped autonomic recovery but did not lower cortisol.

caveats: Effects are averages over people and sessions and are small to moderate.

notEstimated.name: Serotonin
notEstimated.summary: Not estimated: no brain study has measured serotonin release to music.
notEstimated.detail: The only direct study measured serotonin in blood platelets, not the brain: levels differed between pleasant and unpleasant music. Serotonin is often called a 'happiness chemical', but mood depends on far more than one chemical, and nothing links it to particular moments of a song.
